candidates.title: Competing cognitive pathways associated with generative AI tool use and self-reported critical thinking in higher education
candidates.genre: cross-sectional survey and structural equation model
candidates.source_comparison: The authors collected 389 questionnaires from undergraduates at 10 Jiangsu universities and retained 378 after excluding 11. AI use had no significant direct or total association with self-reported critical thinking. The positive indirect path through self-regulated learning (B=0.147, 95% CI 0.096 to 0.212) and negative path through cognitive offloading (B=-0.148, 95% CI -0.219 to -0.092) were nearly equal; a smaller positive sequential path also appeared.
candidates.concrete_example: The paper proposes a thinking-first, AI-second task: record an initial interpretation, consult AI, evaluate its evidence and assumptions, and document any changed judgment. It says this intervention was not tested.
candidates.limit: All focal variables and critical thinking came from one self-report questionnaire at one time point. The paths are associations, not causal mediation, and demonstrated critical-thinking performance was not measured.

candidates.title: Learning Cannot Be Delegated: Why the Division of Cognitive Work Between Learners and Generative AI Should Shift Over Time
candidates.genre: open-access critical review and conceptual framework
candidates.source_comparison: The author argues that AI support should move from performing to proposing to prompting and fade as learners gain skill. Claims that AI improves learning should include unassisted outcomes, learner-process evidence, calibration and preferably durable gains.
candidates.concrete_example: A polished AI-assisted essay shows performance with a tool but does not itself show that the learner performed the operations needed to write or defend the argument.
candidates.limit: This is a critical review, not a systematic review or new experiment. Examples were chosen for significance; the underlying studies differ and mostly measure short-term outcomes.

candidates.title: GenAI-supported self-explanation and its effects on metacognitive monitoring and critical reading comprehension
candidates.source_comparison: Study 1 compared personalized GenAI feedback, self-explanation alone and reading only among 119 students. Study 2 compared scaffolded, standard and no prompts among 113. Feedback improved immediate comprehension in Study 1 but not absolute monitoring accuracy; scaffolded prompts improved explanation quality and monitoring accuracy in Study 2 but not critical-reading comprehension.
candidates.limit: Neither experiment included a delayed or independent-transfer test.

candidates.title: Cognitive load theory and learner competencies as predictors of effective GenAI training for preservice teachers
candidates.source_comparison: A convenience sample of 450 preservice teachers in Spain and Indonesia reported cognitive load, prior knowledge, metacognitive and problem-solving skills, and perceived usefulness while designing GenAI-supported materials.
candidates.limit: The model concerns perceived load and usefulness, not objectively measured load, teaching performance or a training effect; cross-sectional paths do not establish causality.

candidates.title: Why Teacher AI Use Has Plateaued, and What Could Come Next
candidates.source_comparison: A nationally representative survey of 590 teachers found 62% reported at least some classroom AI use, versus 61% in 2025 and 34% in 2023. The measured result is a one-year plateau; explanations about saturation, screen time, guidance and training are attributed to experts.
candidates.limit: The survey measured reported use, not whether AI improved teaching or student learning.

candidates.title: How Aspiring Teachers View AI for Instruction: We Asked Teacher Educators
candidates.source_comparison: Among 268 teacher educators surveyed in August and September, about one quarter said their preservice teachers viewed instructional AI negatively and about two in five said they viewed it positively.
candidates.concrete_example: One special-education course lets students ask AI to test a lesson plan against varied learning needs but offers peer feedback as a non-AI alternative.
candidates.limit: Teacher educators reported perceptions of preservice teachers' views; the survey did not directly sample those aspiring teachers.

candidates.title: Los Angeles schools block Google's AI features, consider dropping tech giant's products
candidates.source_comparison: AP reports that Los Angeles Unified disabled AI Overview on student devices while districts and Google disputed whether ordinary search can remain available without integrated AI. The district called the step temporary and safety-oriented; Google said it shares the learning goal and is developing guided learning.
candidates.concrete_example: The district enrolls about half a million students; parent advocates used videos of school-issued screens before the district confirmed AI Overview was disabled.
candidates.limit: This policy and product-access dispute does not show that disabling summaries improves attention, search skill or learning. Cognitive-effect claims are attributed concerns, not measured outcomes.

candidates.title: How to Turn a Classroom Activity Into an Interactive Learning Sim
candidates.source_comparison: The author argues that instructors can turn an existing activity into a branching simulation. Six instructors in a workshop each built one in 30 minutes.
candidates.concrete_example: An education professor created a case where students diagnose a child's reading difficulty, choose an instructional response and use feedback to decide what to try next.
candidates.limit: The workshop shows feasibility, not a measured learning effect of AI-built simulations.

candidates.title: What Happens When AI Outruns Title I Schools?
candidates.source_comparison: A Title I high-school teacher argues that unclear rules, uneven access and insufficient training produce contradictory messages about AI as a thought partner rather than a generator.
candidates.limit: The examples and proposed plan are the author's experience and argument, not measured outcomes.

candidates.title: Is AI-assisted thinking devaluing business degrees?
candidates.reason: Directly concerns which thinking and judgment a degree develops. The pipeline retrieved 8,364 characters but has not verified semantic completeness, so it remains held.

candidates.title: US schools are moving away from AI in Google searches. Should Australia do the same?
candidates.reason: Potentially relevant to search and source evaluation. The pipeline retrieved 5,226 characters but has not verified semantic completeness; AP is retained separately as the original U.S. reporting source.
